meta.scope: Quad Cortex catalog sections: Guitar Overdrive (46 models, ids 1-52), Compressor, Delay, Modulation, Reverb, plus technique rules covering gates, wah, pitch, post-EQ and stereo.
meta.settings_convention: Role settings use QC parameter names and ranges from qc-catalog.txt (mostly 0..10). basis='cited' means the source states the setting or its direction (e.g. 'drive at zero, level up'); the exact number may be a conversion (clock positions: 7 o'clock=0, noon=5, 5 o'clock=10). basis='typical' means a conventional starting point for that role, not a quoted value. Switch values are descriptive strings because the QC switch encoding is not in the catalog.
source_notes: www.electrosmash.com did not resolve during this research; circuit numbers were read from the mirror at electrosmash.mas-effects.com (same articles).
wiki.fractalaudio.com returned HTTP 403, so no Fractal wiki drive-model notes are included.
Neural DSP plugin manuals name almost no real pedals; where 'real' is empty for a plugin pedal the resemblance is not documented.
Entries tagged 'unsourced-character' describe community consensus that was not confirmed against a fetched page.

drives.name: Myth Drive
drives.signature: Clean path blended with Ge hard-clipped path; gain peaks ~1 kHz (mid hump); treble shelf from ~408 Hz (+18/-8 dB); 18 V rail headroom.

GAIN.does: Dual-gang pot: raises the clipped signal while lowering the clean feed-forward blend, so low GAIN is mostly clean boost.

TREBLE.does: Active high shelf above ~400 Hz, about +18 dB to -8 dB; noon is roughly flat.

LEVEL.does: Output volume (labelled OUTPUT on the pedal); the main control when used as a boost.

drives.watch_out: Designed to work with an amp's own overdrive, not as the only dirt on a sterile clean amp; it cuts far less bass than a TS, so it tightens high-gain amps less.

drives.name: Obsessive Drive
drives.signature: MOSFET clipping, amp-like and full-range with big low end; PEAK HP adds drive, bottom and upper mids, LP stays closer to guitar/amp tone.

PEAK.does: HP/LP = High Peak/Low Peak (not high-pass/low-pass). HP: more drive, volume, bottom and upper-mid emphasis. LP: flatter, closer to the bypassed tone.

TONE.does: Treble roll-off; one source says the PEAK switch also moves its shelving frequency.

DRIVE.does: Gain; wide range from clean-ish push to distortion.

into: clean amps at edge of breakup

drives.watch_out: Full low end and high output: as a boost into a high-gain amp it adds bass and flub instead of tightening; HP mode is a volume jump versus LP.

drives.name: OD250
drives.signature: Op-amp gain into diodes to ground, no tone control; in the near-identical Distortion+ the bass corner climbs to ~720 Hz at max gain.

GAIN.does: Op-amp gain; raising it also raises the bass roll-off corner (3 Hz at minimum to ~720 Hz at maximum in the sister MXR Distortion+ circuit), so more gain = thinner lows.

VOLUME.does: Output level; high output makes it a strong amp pusher.

drives.watch_out: No tone control and the lows thin out as GAIN rises; raspy into bright clean amps. Circuit numbers come from the MXR Distortion+ analysis (the 250 differs mainly in silicon diodes and a few values).

drives.name: Rodent Drive
drives.signature: Op-amp gain to 67 dB, lows below ~1.5 kHz get less gain, Si hard clip, slow LM308 softens highs; FILTER low-pass 475 Hz-32 kHz.

FILTER.does: Passive low-pass after clipping, cutoff ~32 kHz down to ~475 Hz. WORKS BACKWARDS: turning up cuts treble.

DISTORTION.does: Gain 0 to ~67 dB; low = overdrive, above about two-thirds = thick fuzz-like saturation.

drives.watch_out: FILTER is reversed versus every other tone knob (up = darker); any software 'brighter' move must decrease it. Fully up it is extremely dark.

drives.name: Green 808
drives.signature: Lows below 720 Hz get less gain, 723 Hz low-pass after clipping: mid hump around 720 Hz; soft symmetric clip, gain 12x-118x.

OVERDRIVE.does: Clipping-stage gain 12x to 118x (41 dB); even at 0 the pedal still has gain and its bass cut/mid hump.

TONE.does: Active treble control after a fixed 723 Hz low-pass; at maximum it restores highs above ~3.2 kHz, at minimum it removes treble.

LEVEL.does: Output volume; the control that pushes the amp when used as a boost.

drives.watch_out: Cuts lows and adds 700-800 Hz honk: thin and nasal alone into a clean amp, and too much midrange on an amp that is already mid-heavy or tight.

drives.name: Exotic
drives.signature: RC Booster core plus clipping diodes and fixed TS-style mid voicing; active bass/treble boost-cut; most gain of the Xotic trio.

GAIN.does: Slightly dirty to heavily overdriven; compresses as it rises.

drives.watch_out: BASS above noon into a dirty amp adds flub; the EQ is boost/cut, so 'neutral' is 5, not 0.

drives.name: Freeman BOD
drives.signature: Friedman BE-style cascaded high-gain preamp distortion; TIGHT cuts bass before clipping; bass/treble/presence EQ; very high output.

TIGHT.does: Bass cut at the first gain stage, before clipping; up = tighter, less low end into the distortion (forum reading of the schematic).

TRIM.does: Model of the pedal's internal gain trimmer: sets the overall gain range, from vintage-ish to extreme. Owners report running it low (about 8:30-9 o'clock).

PRESENCE.does: Upper-treble cut-through; raise for clarity in a band mix.

BASS.does: Post-distortion low end; interacts with TIGHT.

drives.watch_out: It is a complete high-gain preamp: into an already distorted amp it becomes noisy, fizzy and over-compressed. Keep TRIM and GAIN low and gate it.

drives.name: Brit Blues
drives.signature: Low-gain op-amp soft clipping with an open, un-humped midrange and a low gain ceiling; drive comes on gradually.

GAIN.does: Low overall range; even high settings stay in light-overdrive territory.

TONE.does: Single treble control (no 3-band EQ like the Guv'nor).

drives.watch_out: Low gain and no real bass cut: it will not tighten a high-gain amp and cannot reshape mids.

drives.name: Chief DS1
drives.signature: Transistor booster (35 dB) + op-amp (to 26.5 dB) into Si hard clip; Muff-style tone tilts LP 234 Hz / HP 1063 Hz around a ~500 Hz scoop.

TONE.does: Blends a 234 Hz low-pass against a 1063 Hz high-pass; mids are scooped around 500 Hz at noon. Up = treble side.

DISTORTION.does: Op-amp gain 0 to 26.5 dB on top of a fixed transistor boost; bass corner rises to ~72 Hz at maximum.

LEVEL.does: Output; the circuit loses level internally, so it usually sits well above noon.

drives.watch_out: Scooped around 500 Hz and fizzy above noon TONE, so it can vanish in a band mix into a clean amp; it is the opposite EQ shape to a Tube Screamer.

drives.name: Brit Governor
drives.signature: LED hard clipping (~1.8-2 V, high headroom), ~70 dB total gain, 723 Hz pre-clip high-pass, Marshall-style interactive 3-band stack.

MID.does: FMV-style stack: almost every setting leaves a scoop between 1 and 3 kHz, so MID usually needs to be up.

BASS.does: Passive, interactive with MID and TREBLE.

drives.watch_out: The tone stack is interactive and scooped by default; in front of an already Marshall-voiced dirty amp the voicing doubles up and turns harsh.

drives.name: Chief MT
drives.signature: Dual-stage high gain with seven filters pre/post; active LOW/HIGH +/-15 dB and a +/-15 dB MIDDLE sweepable 200 Hz-5 kHz.

MIDFREQ.does: Sweeps the MIDDLE band from 200 Hz to 5 kHz; behaves almost like a global voicing control.

HIGH.does: Active shelving +/-15 dB; rolling back removes fizz but too far removes upper mids.

drives.watch_out: EQ range is +/-15 dB, so move in small steps from 5; maxed DIST and HIGH is the notorious 'buzzing bees' tone. Start with lower gain than seems necessary.

drives.name: Chief OD1
drives.signature: The original asymmetric soft-clipping overdrive (ancestor of TS and SD-1); no tone control; more bass roll-off than the SD-1.

GAIN.does: Overdrive amount; no tone control exists, so voicing is fixed.

drives.watch_out: No tone control: if the boosted tone is too dark or too nasal the only fix is amp EQ or another pedal.

drives.name: Chief SD1
drives.signature: Asymmetric soft clipping (2 diodes one side, 1 the other); midrange focus ~800 Hz; less bass roll-off than OD-1/TS, so fuller.

TONE.does: Treble control added over the OD-1.

OVERDRIVE.does: Gain; set high it adds grit in front of an already-overdriven amp.

drives.watch_out: Fuller lows than a Tube Screamer, so on an already boomy amp it tightens less.

drives.name: Fuzz Pi
drives.signature: Booster + two cascaded diode-clipping stages; tone blends LP/HP around a ~1 kHz notch (about -13.5 dB total at noon); huge sustain.

TONE.does: Single pot blending a low-pass and a high-pass: down = bass side, up = treble side, mids scooped around 1 kHz in the middle. It can never be flat.

SUSTAIN.does: Level into the clipping stages (gain); high settings hold saturation even from a weak signal.

drives.watch_out: Scooped at ~1 kHz, so it disappears in a band mix; into a distorted amp it turns to mush. Pair it with a mid-forward stage (e.g. a TS) rather than more gain.

drives.name: Chief BD2
drives.signature: Bright, full-range, touch-sensitive overdrive without a pronounced mid hump; cleans up with picking and guitar volume (community consensus).

GAIN.does: Clean-ish boost at low settings through crunchy overdrive.

drives.watch_out: No circuit source was fetched for this model; the usual complaint is brightness/harshness with TONE above noon into a bright amp.

drives.name: Rage Booster
drives.signature: Single germanium transistor, up to 38 dB gain; 5 nF input cap high-passes at ~2.6 kHz so only treble gets full gain; soft clipping.

VOLUME.does: The only control: amount of boost (and, near maximum, soft clipping). There is no tone control; the treble emphasis is fixed.

drives.watch_out: Built to cut the mud from a dark, already-overdriven tube amp; into a clean or bright amp it is thin and shrill. Low input impedance (~10-12 k) means it belongs first in the chain.

drives.name: Facial Fuzz
drives.signature: Two-transistor feedback fuzz; very low input impedance (~5-8 kOhm) loads the pickups, which is why guitar volume cleans it up.

FUZZ.does: Sets second-stage emitter degeneration/feedback: more = more gain and harder clipping. Conventionally run at or near maximum, with the guitar volume used to clean up.

VOLUME.does: Output level; the real circuit has little output gain and lower settings thin the bass.

PICKUP.does: Not documented by Neural DSP. Presumably a pickup-loading simulation for the low-impedance input (unverified).

PICKUP LEVEL.does: Not documented by Neural DSP (unverified; possibly the simulated guitar-volume/pickup level feeding the fuzz).

drives.watch_out: Must be first: a buffer, wah or any pedal in front changes it for the worse (low input impedance). PICKUP / PICKUP LEVEL are undocumented, so software should leave them at defaults.

drives.name: Exotic Z Boost
drives.signature: Clean boost / low-gain preamp with active bass and treble; 'clean to slightly dirty'; BB Preamp core without the clipping diodes.

BASS.does: Active low boost/cut; 5 is flat. Cut it to tighten.

drives.watch_out: Flat and full-range: it only tightens a high-gain amp if BASS is turned down; BASS above noon adds flub.

drives.name: Red Drive
drives.signature: Modded TS9-family overdrive with a FET input stage and Lo/Hi gain modes; TS mid voicing with more range.

MODE.does: Lo/Hi gain. Lo: thicker with more midrange. Hi: fatter with more gain range.

drives.watch_out: Same family caveats as a Tube Screamer (bass cut, mid honk); Hi mode in front of a high-gain amp adds gain and noise rather than tightness.

drives.name: Vemural Ray
drives.signature: Low/medium-gain transparent overdrive voiced after blackface Fender 'Magic 6' tones; less compression and colour than a TS.

BASS.does: Low-frequency control (direction on the model not verified).

TREBLE.does: High-frequency control (direction on the model not verified).

GAIN.does: Light breakup to medium overdrive with natural-feeling compression.

drives.watch_out: Low gain and uncompressed, so not a high-gain tightener; the real pedal's saturation trimmer is not exposed in the QC parameters.

drives.name: No-Bell OD1
drives.signature: 'The other green overdrive': balanced EQ without the TS mid spike and bass cut; SPECTRUM raises highs and lower-mids together.

SPECTRUM.does: Dual filter, not a simple tone knob: turning up boosts highs AND lower-mids at once; turning down cuts both, leaving a more midrange-forward sound.

BASS CUT.does: Trims the low end, which is otherwise prominent with humbuckers (added on later ODR-1 versions).

MUTE TRIG.does: Internal trigger parameter; leave at default.

drives.watch_out: Full low end: without BASS CUT it gets boomy with humbuckers or in front of a dirty amp. SPECTRUM changes two bands at once.

drives.name: Green 808
drives.signature: Second catalog entry with the same name and parameters as id 5: bass cut below 720 Hz, mid hump ~720 Hz, soft clip.

OVERDRIVE.does: Clipping-stage gain 12x to 118x; still coloured at 0.

TONE.does: Active treble control after a fixed 723 Hz low-pass.

drives.watch_out: Duplicate of id 5 in the catalog (which one is current is not documented); same honk/thin-lows caveats.

drives.name: Thunderpaw
drives.signature: High-gain distortion with active bass and treble cut/boost and a wide gain range (very little to a lot).

USE GATE.does: QC-side gate switch; the hardware pedal's documentation found does not mention a gate.

drives.watch_out: A distortion, not a boost: stacking it into a dirty amp multiplies noise. EQ is active boost/cut, so 5 is neutral.

drives.name: MK3 Silicon Fuzz
drives.signature: Silicon take on the 1973 Sola Sound Tone Bender MKIII: three-transistor-style fuzz with a tone sweep; smoother and thicker than a Fuzz Face.

ATTACK.does: The fuzz/distortion amount; more = more fuzz.

TONE.does: Sweeps between dark and bright (which direction is brighter was not verified).

drives.watch_out: TONE direction unverified; the hardware's 'JHS mode' (more gain plus mid boost) is not exposed. Treat like any fuzz: early in the chain, clean-ish amp.

drives.name: Plini Drive
drives.signature: Plugin boost/overdrive 'for tighter rhythms and saturated lead'; MODE switches Overdrive to Fuzz for richer harmonic distortion.
drives.watch_out: No real pedal is named by Neural DSP. Fuzz mode adds harmonic distortion and is not a tightening boost.

drives.name: Cory Wong The Tuber
drives.signature: Neural: 'a modded classic; a booster loved by tube amp fanatics' (name implies a modded Tube Screamer-style circuit; not stated).

BASS.does: Low-end control present on the QC model; not described in the plugin manual v1.0.0.

drives.watch_out: Resemblance to a real pedal is inferred from the name only; BASS is undocumented.

drives.name: Cory Wong The Big Rig Overdrive
drives.signature: Neural: 'a heavy and powerful overdrive pedal that pushes saturation to the beginnings of fuzz'.
drives.watch_out: No real pedal named. Heavy saturation into a clean funk amp can swamp note definition; keep DRIVE moderate.

drives.name: Nolly Overdrive-2
drives.signature: Second 'overdrive/booster' in Archetype: Nolly with gain, bass and treble; a reviewer calls it thicker and beefier, for adding dirt.
drives.watch_out: No real pedal named. In the plugin it sits after Overdrive-1 and Delay-1; stacking both drives with similar EQ can get muddy.

drives.name: Nolly Overdrive-1
drives.signature: First 'overdrive/booster' in Archetype: Nolly; a reviewer calls it the usual green overdrive for tightening; adds a BRIGHT switch.

BRIGHT.does: High-frequency boost for articulation and clarity. Nolly recommends leaving it on unless you want a particularly smooth character.

drives.watch_out: TS-style identity comes from a reviewer, not Neural DSP. With BRIGHT on plus a bright amp, fizz may need a lower TONE or a post low-pass.

drives.name: Gojira DRT
drives.signature: Plugin 'Distortion pedal' with DIST / FILTER / VOL, the RAT control layout; FILTER is a low-pass that darkens as it is raised.

FILTER.does: Manual: 'Low-pass filter control. Increase to reduce the amount of high frequencies.' WORKS BACKWARDS.

drives.watch_out: FILTER is reversed (up = darker), like the RAT. Neural DSP does not name a real pedal; the RAT resemblance is by control layout only.

drives.name: Gojira OD
drives.signature: Plugin 'Overdrive pedal (OD)' with DIST / TONE / LEVEL, placed before the amps for boosting.
drives.watch_out: No real pedal or frequency behaviour is documented, so the amount of low cut is unknown; verify tightness by ear or measurement.

drives.name: SLO-100 Overdrive-2
drives.signature: The 'overdrive (OD2)' of the Soldano suite; HI PEAK switch adds a hi-mid frequency boost.

HI PEAK.does: Manual: activates/deactivates the hi-mid frequency boost.

drives.watch_out: No real pedal named. HI PEAK plus a bright SLO channel can get harsh in the upper mids.

drives.name: SLO-100 Overdrive-1
drives.signature: The 'boost (OD1)' of the Soldano suite: drive/tone/level booster ahead of the amp.

BASS.does: Low-end control present on the QC model; not described in the plugin manual v1.0.0.

drives.watch_out: No real pedal named and BASS is undocumented; do not assume TS-style low cut.

drives.name: Fortin Grind
drives.signature: One-knob boost (marketed up to +20 dB) with fixed bass cut and upper-mid focus; 'adds clarity and articulation' ahead of high gain.

BOOST.does: Single knob = output level of the boost (labelled GRIND in the plugin). The EQ curve is fixed.

drives.watch_out: Cuts a lot of bass and is a character pedal, not a transparent boost; a hobbyist measurement found far less than the claimed +20 dB, so set BOOST by output level, not by a dB assumption.

drives.name: Fortin Hexdrive
drives.signature: Neural: 'an overdrive pedal with a higher output than most, with additional headroom and an irregular style of clipping'.

BASS.does: Low-end control present on the QC model; not described in the plugin manual v1.0.0.

drives.watch_out: Higher output than most overdrives: LEVEL values that suit a TS will hit the amp harder here. BASS is undocumented.

drives.name: 81 Creations Drive
drives.signature: RAT-derived (1985 Whiteface starting point) drive with a fixed-level preamp and far less gain than a RAT; CUT is a treble-cut control.

CUT.does: Treble cut: the further up, the more highs are removed. WORKS BACKWARDS. Interacts with DRV (acts differently at low and high gain).

LEVEL.does: The pedal's volume knob, in percent.

OUTPUT.does: QC block output trim in dB (-60..12); not a pedal control. Keep at 0 dB unless level-matching.

drives.watch_out: CUT is reversed (up = darker) and this is the only drive whose knobs are in percent with a separate dB OUTPUT; scale-sensitive code must special-case it.

drives.name: Petrucci Overdrive
drives.signature: Plugin overdrive pedal (tone/drive/level) ahead of the Petrucci amps; no real pedal or voicing documented.

MODE.does: Present on the QC model; not described in the plugin manual v1.0.0.

drives.watch_out: MODE is undocumented; leave it at default. Voicing unknown, so do not assume TS-style bass cut.

drives.name: John Mayer Halfman OD
drives.real: Klon Centaur (John Mayer's own unit, per Neural DSP)
drives.signature: 'A mid-gain overdrive pedal that pushes amplifiers harder while preserving their natural tone and response.' Klon-style gain/treble/level.

TREBLE.does: Manual: clockwise for brightness, counter-clockwise for darkness.

drives.watch_out: Same family as Myth Drive (id 1): it pushes an amp rather than making all the dirt itself.

drives.name: John Mayer Justa Boost
drives.real: Keeley Katana (per Neural DSP press material)
drives.signature: Boost with two modes: a transparent clean boost and an overdriven boost; used as an always-on thickener for single coils.

BOOST.does: Toggles between the clean boost and the overdrive-style boost mode.

MUTE TRIG.does: Internal trigger parameter; leave at default.

drives.watch_out: Full-range boost with no EQ: it raises bass as much as treble, so it will not tighten a high-gain amp.

drives.name: John Mayer Tealbreaker
drives.real: Marshall Bluesbreaker MK1 + Ibanez TS-10 (per Neural DSP press material)
drives.signature: Dual-circuit overdrive: TS = smooth, mid-focused, rolls off lows; BB = balanced, clear, keeps the amp's character.

MODEL.does: BB/TS switch between the two overdrive circuits.

TONE.does: Manual: clockwise for brightness, counter-clockwise for darkness.

drives.watch_out: The two MODEL positions are different pedals: the same knob values do not transfer when the switch changes.

drives.name: Rabea Colossus Fuzz
drives.signature: Two-circuit fuzz: 'the raw character of vintage fuzz with the tighter, more defined response of a modern design'; bass/treble EQ.

MUTE TRIG.does: Internal trigger parameter; leave at default.

drives.watch_out: No real pedals named. Vintage mode is the looser one; into a high-gain amp either mode gets woolly.

drives.name: Rabea Paragon Overdrive
drives.signature: Two circuits: vintage mode is a mid-focused overdrive; modern mode is 'more transparent and dynamic'; bass/treble EQ.
drives.watch_out: No real pedals named; choose MODE by role (Vintage for mid-push boosting, Modern for transparent drive).

drives.name: Misha Chaos
drives.signature: Custom DIY pedal inspired by a classic Swedish-metal distortion (HM-2 'chainsaw' style), made to front high-gain amps; clean blend.

MIX.does: Blends the distorted signal with the clean signal (0..10). There is no gain or tone control.

drives.watch_out: Only two parameters and OUTPUT is in dB, not 0..10; high MIX into a high-gain amp is very noisy and saturated, so gate after it.

drives.name: Horizon Devices Precision Drive
drives.signature: 'Inspired by a well-known green pedal, modified for use as a boost with high-gain amps'; ATTACK sets low-end cut; built-in gate.

ATTACK.does: Stepped (rotary) control for the amount of low frequencies: higher = tighter, more picking clarity; lower = more low-mid punch. Neural recommends a fairly high setting to tighten the amp.

BRIGHT.does: Brightness; turn up until the tone cuts. Intentionally strong and can get harsh at the top of its range on mid/low-gain tones.

GATE.does: Sensitivity of the built-in noise gate; 0 = gate fully bypassed. Low just removes noise; high gives a very tight, choppy stop.

drives.watch_out: ATTACK is a rotary switch, not a 0..10 knob; BRIGHT and ATTACK are set by ear after DRIVE/VOLUME. Cranked GATE chokes sustain; reviewers note fizzy edges when pushed.

drives.name: Tim Henson Overdrive
drives.signature: 'Based on a classic overdrive circuit with a pronounced midrange character'; adds warmth, grit and saturation.

BASS.does: Low-end control present on the QC model; not described in the plugin manual.

drives.watch_out: The 'classic circuit' is not named (TS-style is implied by the midrange description only); BASS is undocumented.

drives.name: Tim Henson Boost
drives.signature: 'A transparent clean boost that increases gain without coloring your tone'; doubles as an overdrive; bass/treble EQ.
drives.watch_out: Transparent means no built-in bass cut: to tighten, BASS must be lowered deliberately.

rules.rule: To tighten a high-gain amp, put an overdrive in front with drive at or near zero, level high, tone around noon.
rules.why: The aim is to shape and tighten the amp's existing distortion, not to add more; the pedal's level pushes the preamp while its EQ pre-shapes the signal.

numbers.tone: 5/10, raise for clarity, lower to thicken

rules.rule: Prefer a Tube Screamer-family pedal for the tightening boost because it cuts bass before clipping and pushes mids.
rules.why: In a TS only harmonics above 720 Hz get the full clipping gain (20 dB/decade less below) and a 723 Hz low-pass follows, giving a mid hump. Low end overdrives before high end, so removing bass before the amp's gain stages stops flubby, smeared palm mutes.

rules.rule: Explain the boost to users as 'less bass into the distortion', not 'more gain'.
rules.why: Kurt Ballou: an overdrive's feedback path cuts lows, so the amp receives less bass; low end tends to overdrive before high end. Pete Thorn: TS-type pedals cut bass and boost mids, making the tone more defined and tight at once.

rules.rule: Skip or soften the boost when the amp is already tight and bright, or when the result turns thin, nasal or noisy.
rules.why: Amps with an inherently tight low end do not need a boost (Guitar World cites the ENGL Fireball); a mid-hump pedal on a mid-heavy amp stacks honk around 800 Hz, and every boost raises hiss so the gate has to work harder.

rules.rule: When a boost is engaged, lower the amp's gain and bass rather than leaving them where they were.
rules.why: 'As the gain control goes up, cut the bass' and 'start low and raise gain gradually'; at higher gain bass gets flubby, so amp bass often needs to be lower than expected. Boost plus reduced amp gain keeps saturation with better note definition.

rules.rule: For the Precision Drive start with DRIVE fully down and VOLUME at about three quarters, raise BRIGHT until it cuts, then set ATTACK by ear, GATE low.
rules.why: Manufacturer starting point; the pedal is voiced to tighten high-gain heads and modelers, including low tunings and extended-range guitars. Higher ATTACK = less low end = tighter.

numbers.GATE: low for noise only; high for a very tight stop; 0 = bypassed

rules.rule: Choose the boost by how much low cut is needed: TS/OD-1 (most), SD-1 (less, fuller), Klon or clean boost (little unless BASS is turned down).
rules.why: The SD-1 is centred around 800 Hz with less bass roll-off than the OD-1 and TS, so it sounds fuller; the Klon's shelving treble starts at ~408 Hz and it keeps a clean blend, so its lows stay largely intact.

rules.rule: Use a treble booster only into an amp that is already overdriven and on the dark side.
rules.why: The Rangemaster high-passes at ~2.6 kHz and adds up to 38 dB; it was designed because British amps (AC30, JTM45) got dark and muddy when overdriven. Into a clean or bright amp the same curve is thin and shrill.

rules.rule: Stack lower-gain pedals before higher-gain ones and use the level controls to trim.
rules.why: A low-gain stage into a higher-gain one adds clarity while keeping saturation; the first pedal's level sets how hard the second is hit.

rules.rule: Reverse the order (high gain into low gain) only when a more compressed, sustaining sound is wanted.
rules.why: The second stage then compresses an already saturated signal instead of pre-shaping it.

rules.rule: Do not stack two drives that boost the same frequency band; offset their tone controls and balance their levels.
rules.why: Overlapping EQ emphasis (e.g. two mid-hump pedals) results in a muddy sound; unbalanced levels cause volume jumps when either is switched.

rules.rule: Put a boost before a drive for more saturation and after it for a louder lead with no extra clipping.
rules.why: Before: the boost drives the next stage into more clipping and a fatter tone. After: it raises level without adding clipping (only works while the amp has headroom).

rules.rule: Pair a mid-scooped fuzz or distortion (Big Muff, DS-1) with a mid-forward gain stage instead of adding more gain.
rules.why: The Big Muff notches about 1 kHz (-13.5 dB total at noon) and the DS-1 about 500 Hz, so they disappear in a band mix; a second stage with mids restores cut.

rules.rule: Keep fuzz, treble booster and octave-fuzz at the very front, before buffers and other pedals.
rules.why: These circuits interact directly with the pickups: the Fuzz Face input impedance is only ~5-8 kOhm and the Rangemaster ~10-12 kOhm; a buffer in front makes a germanium Fuzz Face sound 'awful'.

rules.rule: Place the gate before delay and reverb, never after them.
rules.why: A gate after time-based effects treats the tails as noise and cuts them off.

rules.rule: For high gain, gate after the gain stages but key the gate from the clean guitar signal (four-cable / side-chain method).
rules.why: An in-line gate before the amp cannot remove preamp hiss, and an in-line gate after it sees guitar and hiss as one signal. Detecting on the clean input while attenuating after the preamp is more effective. On the QC this is Adaptive Gate (S/C) placed after the amp with SOURCE = the guitar input.

rules.rule: Set the threshold by raising it from minimum until idle noise just disappears, then stop.
rules.why: A threshold set higher than needed chops note decay and pinch harmonics; some residual noise is better than truncated sustain. If only an extreme gate makes the patch usable, the gain is too high.

numbers.procedure: start at lowest, increase until noise disappears; decay/release from shortest upward for natural tails

rules.rule: Use one gate per path on the Quad Cortex: do not leave the Input Gate active when adding a gate block.
rules.why: Community reports: two gates with different thresholds interact and cut off pinch harmonics; even at 0 % an enabled gate still clamps, so disable it rather than zero it. A single adaptive gate keyed from Input 1 fixed the problem.

rules.rule: Use hard gating only for fast high-gain rhythm; use gentle reduction (or none) for cleans, single coils and sustained leads.
rules.why: A gate clamps everything below threshold and can sound artificial or muffled; reduction-style suppression preserves natural decay. Players commonly switch the gate off on clean scenes.

rules.rule: If phaser or flanger swoosh is audible when not playing, place the gate after the modulation.
rules.why: A gate after modulation mutes the constant whoosh of flangers and phasers during silences.

rules.rule: Put the compressor at the start of the chain (after wah/pitch, before drives).
rules.why: It sends a consistent signal into everything after it. After boosts, drives or fuzz it amplifies their noise; after modulation or delay it flattens their depth.

rules.rule: Never place a pedal-style compressor after a noisy gain stage; if post-amp levelling is wanted use a gentle studio-style compressor after the cab and before delay/reverb.
rules.why: Gain pedals generate noise that a following compressor boosts. A post-cab bus compressor levels the finished tone, and keeping it ahead of delay and reverb avoids pumping the tails (community practice).

rules.rule: Funk / tight clean rhythm: medium threshold, about 4:1, fast attack, quick release, output matched to bypass.
rules.why: Fast attack keeps strum transients from overwhelming the mix; quick release lets the compressor reset between notes.

rules.rule: Country chicken-pickin' squish: use the highest ratio or the fastest attack the compressor offers, with plenty of sustain.
rules.why: Heavy, fast compression evens out hybrid-picked snaps and gives the characteristic percussive 'pop' followed by bloom.

rules.rule: Smooth lead sustain: about 2:1, slightly lower threshold, slower attack, medium release, level slightly above unity.
rules.why: The slower attack keeps pick bite while the body of the note is held up; medium release avoids unnatural pumping.

rules.rule: Always-on light compression: low ratio with the threshold only catching peaks, and use MIX/BLEND to keep dry dynamics.
rules.why: Subtle compression polishes cleans without removing playing dynamics; a blend control mixes the uncompressed signal back in (parallel compression). No sourced MIX percentage was found.

rules.rule: With high-gain tones use little or no pre-amp compression; if any, 6:1 or higher with a high threshold that touches only the loudest peaks.
rules.why: Distortion already compresses; extra compression mainly raises noise and can make distortion overly pronounced or muted. Fast attack, quick release so sustain is unaffected.

rules.rule: Slapback: 80-140 ms, feedback 0 (one repeat), repeat level around 50 %.
rules.why: Modelled on a tape slap; a single audible repeat thickens without rhythmic clutter. BOSS gives a wider 20-200 ms window with one or two repeats and a low mix.

rules.rule: Doubling/thickening: 50-100 ms with one or two repeats; 20-50 ms gives pseudo chorus/flange.
rules.why: Very short delays fuse with the dry note and read as a second guitar or as comb-filter colour rather than an echo.

rules.rule: For delays over 200 ms in tempo-based music, sync to tempo using ms = factor / bpm.
rules.why: Above ~200 ms repeats are heard as distinct notes, so off-tempo repeats clash with the beat.

rules.rule: Dotted-eighth rhythmic delay: sync to a dotted eighth, set the repeat as loud as the dry note, keep feedback low, and play short straight eighths.
rules.why: A dotted eighth is 1.5 eighth notes, so each repeat lands between the picked eighths and creates a sixteenth-note pattern; long notes or many repeats blur it.

rules.rule: Lead delay: 300-500 ms, two or three repeats, low mix.
rules.why: Adds fullness and sustain behind a solo without overwhelming the tone. If a solo sounds washed out, lower the level before the feedback. Forum figures for lead mix run 20-40 %; 15-25 % is the conservative end.

rules.rule: Pick analog or tape delay when repeats should sit behind the playing, digital when they must stay precise.
rules.why: Analog (BBD) repeats are warm and dark and degrade with each pass; tape repeats are warm, slightly unstable with flutter and degrade further; digital repeats are pristine and only get quieter.

rules.rule: Place delay after all gain (after the amp and cab on a modeler); avoid delay into distortion unless the smeared sound is intended.
rules.why: Before distortion every repeat is distorted and compressed up in level; after the preamp (effects loop / post-amp) the repeats stay clean. Community default on the QC: time-based effects after the amp, everything else before.

rules.rule: Put reverb after delay.
rules.why: Reverb after the delays keeps each repeat distinct and then blends them into the space; delay after reverb repeats the whole wash.

rules.rule: Band-limit the repeats with the delay's HIGH PASS and LOW PASS so they stay out of the dry guitar's way.
rules.why: Mixing practice: aggressive high-pass filtering on a delay keeps it from adding low-mid clutter; rolling off highs pushes repeats back. No sourced Hz values were found; QC delays expose HIGH PASS 20-800 Hz and LOW PASS 1-16 kHz (tape models stop at 6 kHz).

rules.rule: Use the delay's dynamics/ducking section for busy leads so repeats drop while playing and return in the gaps.
rules.why: A ducking (dynamic) delay lets the repeats sit back so they do not step on the notes being played, allowing a higher mix. No sourced depth values were found.

rules.rule: Ambient delay: long time, high feedback, low mix, usually feeding a reverb.
rules.why: The echoes then form a wash behind the playing instead of distinct repeats.

rules.rule: After dialling delay or reverb by ear, pull the mix back by 10-25 %.
rules.why: Engineers and players tend to exaggerate time-based effects in the moment; what sounds right solo is too wet in a mix.

rules.rule: Enable TRAILS on delays and reverbs that are switched during a song.
rules.why: Trails let echoes decay naturally after the effect is turned off instead of cutting out, giving seamless transitions.

rules.rule: Use pre-delay to keep the dry attack clear: about 40-100 ms on guitar; use zero pre-delay to sink a part back into the mix.
rules.why: Pre-delay separates the direct sound from the onset of the tail; with none, the sound blends into the reverb. Values under 20 ms with an audible first reflection can sound phasey.

rules.rule: High-pass and low-pass the reverb itself.
rules.why: Low-frequency reverb energy creates mud; filtering lows out of the reverb lets the low-mids of the dry parts through, and a low-pass makes the tail more natural and less splashy. SOS patches use low-frequency damping around 100 Hz (plate/small room) and low-pass between 3 and 10 kHz.

rules.rule: Match decay to the reverb type: ambience 0.1-1 s, small room ~1-1.6 s, plate ~2.7 s (natural plates 3-4 s), halls 2-10 s.
rules.why: These are the ranges the algorithms are meant to cover; longer decays on dense or fast material wash it out.

rules.rule: Choose reverb type by genre: spring for surf/country/blues/vintage cleans, plate for classic studio and 80s leads, hall for ballads and ambient, room/ambience for rock and metal rhythm, near-dry for grunge and tight metal.
rules.why: Specific spring tanks and plates evoke specific eras and genres; early-digital hall/plate units evoke pop decades; 90s grunge was much drier. Keep spring mix low because it crowds a mix quickly.

rules.rule: Ambient pads: long hall or modulated reverb with the top rolled off as a dark bed; add shimmer sparingly for an octave-up halo.
rules.why: A dark tail sits behind the dry guitar; shimmer adds pitch-shifted (typically +12) harmonics to the reverberated sound and builds quickly with feedback.

rules.rule: Keep reverb last (after delay and after the cab); place it before drive only for deliberate shoegaze/dark washes.
rules.why: Distorting a reverb tail compresses and smears it into a wall, which is the shoegaze sound but wrecks clarity elsewhere.

rules.rule: Default: place chorus, phaser and flanger after drive/amp and before delay and reverb.
rules.why: Distorting a modulated signal smears it and loses definition, especially chorus; after the gain the sweep is clear and consistent.

rules.rule: For the Van Halen sound put the phaser or flanger before the distorted amp, at a slow rate.
rules.why: EVH got all his distortion from the amp, so the phaser ran into it: the result is a smoother, warmer, thicker jet-like sweep that is less dramatic than post-distortion phasing.

rules.rule: Clean chorus: keep rate and depth at or below half; for a lead thickener use rate about half and depth a little lower.
rules.why: Above noon the pitch wobble becomes seasick; a slow rate with moderate depth gives the 80s clean shimmer.

rules.rule: Flanger: for the EVH style use a moderate-fast rate, slightly higher depth and gentle regeneration; for the jet sweep use slow rate with high depth and regeneration.
rules.why: Regeneration (feedback) sets how metallic and resonant the sweep is; slow rate with high feedback gives the long jet whoosh.

rules.rule: Place a Uni-Vibe before fuzz or drive for the Hendrix/Trower sound.
rules.why: Community convention: the vibe's phasey throb is then thickened by the following gain stage rather than chopping the distorted tone. Not confirmed against a fetched source in this research.

rules.rule: Place tremolo after other modulation (and after gain).
rules.why: Tremolo is amplitude modulation; before a compressing gain stage its depth is flattened, and after other modulation it chops the finished sound cleanly.

rules.rule: Treat rotary as a two-speed effect (slow chorale / fast tremolo) and automate the SPEED switch rather than the rate.
rules.why: The musical gesture of a Leslie is the acceleration between the two speeds; the QC Rotary exposes SLOW SPEED, FAST SPEED and ACCELERATION for this. Usage convention not confirmed against a fetched source.

rules.rule: Put wah first, before drive, for the classic vocal sweep; put it after drive or fuzz only for an extreme filter effect.
rules.why: Before gain the wah acts as a tone filter feeding the distortion (Hendrix-style); after gain it sweeps the full harmonic content and is far more dramatic. Never put a wah in front of a Fuzz Face-type model: its low input impedance reacts badly.

rules.rule: Put pitch shifters, octavers and harmonizers at the very front (pitch before wah), ahead of all gain.
rules.why: Pitch tracking works best on the clean, unprocessed signal and may fail on a signal already processed by filters or distortion; following drives also smooth the pitch artifacts.

rules.rule: High-pass the finished guitar tone at about 70-100 Hz.
rules.why: Content below ~70 Hz is rumble that causes muddiness and clashes with bass and kick; the guitar's lowest fundamental is ~82 Hz. Modeler users most often start at 80 Hz, some at 100 Hz.

rules.rule: Low-pass distorted modeler tones somewhere between 5 and 10 kHz, and stop as soon as the fizz is gone.
rules.why: Neural DSP advises cutting above 10 kHz to reduce harshness and buzziness; modeler users report 6.5-8 kHz typical and ~5 kHz as the aggressive end, warning that 6-8 kHz already removes the cab's natural air.

rules.rule: Use this frequency map for corrective moves: mud 200-400 Hz, boxiness 400-800 Hz (up to 1 kHz), honk ~800 Hz, bite 2.5-4 kHz, presence ~5 kHz, fizz/buzz above ~6-10 kHz, air above 10 kHz.
rules.why: Compiled from mixing references: mud/boom 200-400 Hz, boxy 400-800 Hz or 500 Hz-1 kHz, 'green pedal honk' ~800 Hz, bite ~2.5-4 kHz, articulation ~5 kHz, buzziness above 10 kHz. The 'fizz at 6-8 kHz' label is forum usage rather than an official figure.

rules.rule: Keep corrective cuts to about 2-5 dB and tonal boosts to about 1-6 dB.
rules.why: Neural DSP genre starting points: classic rock 400 Hz -2 to -3 dB and 3 kHz +3 to +6 dB; high-gain metal 250-500 Hz -3 to -5 dB, 3 kHz +3 to +5 dB, 5 kHz +4 to +6 dB (leads); cleans 80 Hz +2 to +4 dB, 800 Hz +1 to +3 dB, 6 kHz +1 to +2 dB.

rules.rule: Distinguish pre-amp EQ from post-amp EQ: before the amp it changes how the amp distorts, after it changes only the tone.
rules.why: An EQ after the drives cuts problem bands; early in the chain it acts as an extra gain stage for specific bands (a low cut before the amp tightens, a mid boost adds saturation there).

rules.rule: On the QC implement the cuts with the Low-High Cut block (id 4003) or the IR loader's HI PASS / LOW PASS, and reserve the Parametric EQs for band moves.
rules.why: The catalog exposes HPF/LPF with selectable slopes on Low-High Cut (20 Hz-20 kHz) and HI PASS 20-800 Hz / LOW PASS 1-20 kHz on IR loaders; stock cab-sim blocks list no Hz filters.

rules.rule: Prefer a real second performance for double-tracked width; use the Doubler / Haas delay only as a secondary effect.
rules.why: Two real takes summed to mono just sound thicker; a delayed copy of the same take comb-filters in mono, so parts can change tone or level or vanish.

rules.rule: When using a Haas-style doubler, keep the spread short and the delayed side several dB lower.
rules.why: Haas widening uses roughly 1-40 ms between hard-panned copies; an ~11 ms zero-feedback delay is reported as transparent with good mono compatibility, and dropping the delayed side 3-6 dB (up to 6-10 dB) greatly reduces mono comb filtering. QC Doubler SPREAD is 3-60 ms.

rules.rule: Always check the patch summed to mono; if the output feeds a mono PA or a single cab, disable Doubler, ping-pong and width tricks.
rules.why: Comb filtering appears whenever the two channels are summed, and even from stereo speakers placed close together; ping-pong repeats double in density and wide chorus partly cancels.

rules.rule: Keep the core tone mono through the amp and cab and put stereo (ST) modulation, delay and reverb after the cab.
rules.why: A mono block after a stereo effect collapses its width, and amp/cab models are mono sources. Convention; not confirmed against a fetched Neural DSP document.

rules.rule: For width without phase risk use different delay times left and right or a stereo chorus/dimension effect rather than a short Haas offset.
rules.why: Long, clearly different delay times (BOSS example: 12 ms one side, 800 ms the other) or decorrelated modulation create space without the comb filtering of a single short offset.
